title: ErrorEnvelope
description: The error body every non-OAuth route answers with, derived from identity_cloudflare::error::ErrorEnvelope. `code` is the contract a client branches on; `message` is not, and changes whenever the wording improves. `client_safe` records whether the message on the wire is the error's own text or the generic substitute, so an operator reading a captured response can tell WHICH rule downgraded it. The code set and the status mapping below are the documented error contract, derived from HttpStatus::for_code.
x-serde-status: the envelope type is IMPLEMENTED as a shape; no Worker emits it yet, because all three Worker composition roots are placeholders

code.description: The stable machine-readable code, mapped to an HTTP status by HttpStatus::for_code. A client branches on this and never on the message.

x-accepted-values.source: ApplicationError::code, SecurityError::code and TransportError::code; the union of the three is the client-visible vocabulary
x-accepted-values.constraining: the field is a String in Rust; anything unrecognised maps to 500, because an unmapped code is a gap in the table and the safe reading of a gap is 'our fault', never 'the caller did something wrong'

message.description: The human-readable message, safe to display. When the source error is NOT client-safe this is the fixed generic substitute OPAQUE_MESSAGE — "the request could not be completed" — which says nothing about what failed. A caller learns the code, which is stable and safe to branch on, and learns nothing about our internals; the real reason is logged server-side under the request id.

x-accepted-values.source: identity_cloudflare::error::OPAQUE_MESSAGE == "the request could not be completed" — used whenever client_safe is false
x-accepted-values.constraining: a String in Rust; it is never format!("{inner}") for an operator-facing error, which is the whole point of the substitution

request_id.description: The request identifier, when the transport had one. Omitted from the body entirely when absent, not serialised as null.

client_safe.description: Whether the message is the error's own text rather than the generic substitute. Always false for anything the layers call operator-facing: a Dependency failure, a missing binding, a missing secret, a cryptographic reason, a rate-limiter outage.

429: TooManyRequests is in the closed set but NO code maps to it — the rate limiter fails closed with temporarily_unavailable, which is 503

the-two-500-exceptions.not_implemented: ErrorEnvelope::status() returns 500 for this code, but a declared route answers 501 from the route table with a hand-built response. The status in error.rs is NOT the status on the wire for a declared-but-unimplemented route. See not-implemented-envelope.schema.json.
the-two-500-exceptions.payload_too_large: TransportError::BodyTooLarge maps to the string 'payload_too_large', which is not a row in for_code and therefore falls through to 500. That is the table's documented behaviour for an unmapped code, not an oversight in this file.

x-status-mapping.closed-set: The numeric statuses the platform answers with are exactly 400, 401, 403, 404, 409, 429, 500, 503. A path that could produce any other u16 would let a new variant pick an arbitrary status.

x-internal-collapse.rule: MissingBinding, MissingSecret and Platform collapse to one client-visible code
x-internal-collapse.why: they are three different internal causes with one client-visible answer, and a client that can tell them apart is a client being told which of our internals is misconfigured. The distinction survives where it is useful — the Debug and Display arms, and the log fields a failure is paged from.
x-internal-collapse.source: identity_cloudflare::error::TransportError::code — the three variants share one match arm, and the comment above it says so
x-internal-collapse.same-collapse-elsewhere: ApplicationError::Dependency also maps to 'internal_error', and SecurityError::MissingSecret and ::Cryptographic do as well. All of them send OPAQUE_MESSAGE with client_safe false.
